audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Press 2009:431 passage is verbatim in the held archive.org text of Ball & Mueller 2009 (lines 21772ff, page break to 432 right after). (2) Deciding source is a 2009 grammar sketch by the reference-grammar author, and we additionally hold Kennard 2021 (Phonology 38:363-399), an acoustic/metrical study of exactly this parameter, which states penultimate stress in KLT with a small closed set of final-stress lexical exceptions (historical compounds, -aat/-aer contractions, recent French loans) and analyses it as right-aligned syllabic trochees, quantity-insensitive; older speakers produce 92.5% penult. This matches kind=fixed-strict, rule penult, domain WORD. (3) Nothing in Glottolog's list or the web search (Kennard 2024 TPS; Iosad's Bothoa work; Vannetais dialect theses) suggests a different coding for the standard/KLT variety; the only systematic deviation is

sources.citation: Press, Ian. 2009. 'Breton', ch. 10 of M. J. Ball & N. Müller (eds.), The Celtic Languages, 2nd edn, Routledge (Language Family Series), Phonology section, p. 431. Accessed as freely downloadable full text on archive.org, item 'the-celtic-languages' (The Celtic); full stress passa…
sources.quote: "In KLT the stress is overall on the last-but-one syllable (except in stressable monosyllabics) and is very salient (in Gwenedeg notably the stress is overall final). There are a few words where the stress is final — these are usually compounds." (Press 2009: 431; the chapter then lists final-stressed exceptions adapted from Press 1986: 26-7, e.g. abardaez 'evening', itron 'lady', emaon 'I am', ganin 'with me', and end-stressed place-names with monosyllabic second components.)
